prompt: how does cross-validation detect overfitting?
title: Cross-Validation and Overfitting
body:
When a model memorizes training noise instead of learning general patterns, it suffers from overfitting. To catch this, we use $k$-fold cross-validation by splitting our dataset into multiple subsets.

Look for the validation error curve in this plot to see where generalization degrades.

```rh-diagram

```

The training error continues to fall as model complexity increases, but the validation error reaches a minimum and then rises.

This divergence exposes overfitting because the model fails to generalize to unseen data partitions.

prompt: what is gini impurity
title: Gini Impurity
body:
Gini impurity measures how often a randomly chosen element from a set would be incorrectly labeled if it were randomly labeled according to the distribution of labels in the set.

For a node with $J$ classes, the impurity is calculated as $I_G(p) = 1 - \sum_{i=1}^{J} p_i^2$, where $p_i$ is the probability of a randomly chosen item belonging to class $i$.

Notice how the curve peaks at $0.5$ when classes are evenly split, representing maximum uncertainty.

```rh-diagram
{"version":1,"diagram":{"title":"Gini Impurity for a Two-Class Node","kind":"coordinate-plot","x":{"label":"Probability $p$ of class 1","min":0,"max":1},"y":{"label":"Gini impurity $I_G(p)$","min":0,"max":0.5},"series":[{"label":"$1 - (p^2 + (1-p)^2)$","kind":"line","points":[{"x":0,"y":0},{"x":0.2,"y":0.32},{"x":0.4,"y":0.48},{"x":0.5,"y":0.5,"label":"Max impurity"},{"x":0.6,"y":0.48},{"x":0.8,"y":0.32},{"x":1,"y":0}]}]}}
```

As the probability shifts toward pure nodes where one class dominates, the impurity drops cleanly to zero.

Decision trees use this metric at every split to determine the best feature for separating classes.

title: Turning scores into the next word
body:
When a language model processes a sequence like the cat sat, it outputs a raw score for every possible next word in its vocabulary.

These raw scores are called logits, representing how strongly the model favors each candidate before making its final choice.

Look at the resulting probabilities in the chart to see how the highest bar corresponds to the predicted word.

```rh-diagram
{"version":1,"diagram":{"title":"Vocabulary logits and softmax probabilities","caption":"Raw logits are normalized into probabilities, where on has the highest chance.","kind":"bar-chart","unit":"prob","bars":[{"label":"the","value":0.134},{"label":"cat","value":0.073},{"label":"sat","value":0.178},{"label":"on","value":0.465},{"label":"mat","value":0.1},{"label":"slept","value":0.05}]}}
```

To turn these unconstrained scores into valid probabilities that sum to $1$, the model applies the softmax function.

This exponentiates each logit and divides it by the sum of all exponentiated scores, heavily rewarding higher values.

body:
When building decision trees, algorithms measure node purity using two main metrics: Gini impurity and entropy.

Suppose we have a binary classification task where $p$ is the fraction of items belonging to the first class. Both metrics reach zero when the node is pure ($p=0$ or $p=1$) and peak when the classes are evenly mixed.

Samples rounded to 3 decimals.","kind":"coordinate-plot","x":{"label":"Class fraction p","min":0,"max":1},"y":{"label":"Impurity score","min":0,"max":1},"series":[{"label":"Gini impurity","kind":"line","points":[{"x":0,"y":0},{"x":0.1,"y":0.18},{"x":0.2,"y":0.32},{"x":0.3,"y":0.42},{"x":0.4,"y":0.48},{"x":0.5,"y":0.5,"label":"Gini peak"},{"x":0.6,"y":0.48},{"x":0.7,"y":0.42},{"x":0.8,"y":0.32},{"x":0.9,"y":0.18},{"x":1,"y":0}]},{"label":"Entropy","kind":"line","points":[{"x":0,"y":0},{"x":0.1,"y":0.469},{"x":0.2,"y":0.722},{"x":0.3,"y":0.881},{"x":0.4,"y":0.971},{"x":0.5,"y":1,"label":"Entropy peak"},{"x":0.6,"y":0.971},{"x":0.7,"y":0.881},{"x":0.8,"y":0.722},{"x":0.9,"y":0.469},{"x":1,"y":0}]}]}}

Notice in the plot how both curves are symmetric parabola-like shapes with a maximum at $p=0.5$. Gini impurity calculates the probability of misclassification and peaks at $0.5$.

Entropy measures information disorder in bits and peaks at $1.0$. Because their shapes align closely, choosing between them rarely changes the resulting tree structure.

prompt: what does the sigmoid activation function do?
title: The Sigmoid Activation Function
body:
The sigmoid activation function maps any real-valued number into a bounded range between zero and one.

Its mathematical formula is defined as $\sigma(z) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-z}}$, where $z$ represents the linear score input from a model layer.

```rh-diagram
{"version":1,"diagram":{"title":"A sigmoid links score to probability","caption":"Illustrative values; the geometry shows the stated relationship.","kind":"coordinate-plot","x":{"label":"Linear score","min":-4,"max":4,"scale":"linear"},"y":{"label":"Positive probability","min":0,"max":1},"series":[{"label":"Sigmoid","kind":"line","points":[{"x":-4,"y":0.018},{"x":-3,"y":0.047},{"x":-2,"y":0.119},{"x":-1,"y":0.269},{"x":0,"y":0.5},{"x":1,"y":0.731},{"x":2,"y":0.881},{"x":3,"y":0.953},{"x":4,"y":0.982}]}],"annotations":[{"kind":"reference-line","label":"Probability threshold","axis":"y","value":0.5},{"kind":"reference-line","label":"Equivalent score threshold","axis":"x","value":0}]}}
```

Looking at the plot above, notice how extreme positive scores compress toward one and extreme negative scores compress toward zero.

This S-shaped curve lets models turn raw scores into probabilities for binary classification tasks.

A key limitation in practice is vanishing gradients, where derivatives approach zero for very large positive or negative inputs. This saturation stalls weight updates during backpropagation in deep neural networks.

prompt: what is cross entropy
title: What is cross entropy
body:
Imagine guessing whether a coin landed on heads or tails. Cross entropy is a score that measures how wrong a model's guess is compared to the true fact.

Look at the table below to see how true events and predicted guesses are compared side by side.

```rh-diagram

When the model is completely sure and correct, the penalty score is zero. If the model assigns a low probability to what actually happened, the score grows very large.

prompt: what is cross entropy loss?
title: Cross-Entropy Loss
body:
When a model predicts a cat picture has a probability $p = 0.9$ of being a cat, but the true label is $y = 1$, we need a way to measure how wrong the model is.

Cross-entropy loss penalizes confident wrong answers heavily by taking the negative log of the predicted probability for the correct class, defined as $H(p,y) = -y \log p - (1-y)\log(1-p)$.

Observe how the loss curve shoots upward as the prediction moves away from the true label in the plot.

```rh-diagram
{"version":1,"diagram":{"title":"Cross-entropy depends on the true label","caption":"Illustrative values; the geometry shows the stated relationship.","kind":"coordinate-plot","x":{"label":"Predicted positive probability","min":0.01,"max":0.99,"scale":"linear"},"y":{"label":"Loss","min":0,"max":5},"series":[{"label":"True class 1","kind":"line","points":[{"x":0.01,"y":4.605},{"x":0.1,"y":2.303},{"x":0.25,"y":1.386},{"x":0.5,"y":0.693},{"x":0.75,"y":0.288},{"x":0.9,"y":0.105},{"x":0.99,"y":0.01}]},{"label":"True class 0","kind":"line","points":[{"x":0.01,"y":0.01},{"x":0.1,"y":0.105},{"x":0.25,"y":0.288},{"x":0.5,"y":0.693},{"x":0.75,"y":1.386},{"x":0.9,"y":2.303},{"x":0.99,"y":4.605}]}],"annotations":[]}}
```

For a true class of 1, predicting near zero yields a massive loss, while predicting near one yields near zero loss.

This logarithmic scoring rule forces models to calibrate their confidence rather than just making guesses.

prompt: what is gradient descent?
title: Gradient Descent
body:
Gradient descent is an iterative optimization algorithm used to find the minimum of a function by adjusting parameters in the direction of steepest descent.

Suppose we train a linear model and measure its error using a quadratic loss function $L(w)$.

```rh-diagram
{"version":1,"diagram":{"title":"A descent path on a quadratic loss","caption":"Illustrative values; the geometry shows the stated relationship.","kind":"coordinate-plot","x":{"label":"Weight 1","min":-3,"max":3,"scale":"linear"},"y":{"label":"Weight 2","min":-3,"max":3},"series":[{"label":"Outer loss contour","kind":"line","closed":true,"samples":{"radius":2,"count":16}},{"label":"Inner loss contour","kind":"line","closed":true,"samples":{"radius":1,"count":16}}],"annotations":[{"kind":"vector","label":"Step 1","from":{"x":-1.5,"y":1.1},"to":{"x":-0.9,"y":0.7}},{"kind":"vector","label":"Step 2","from":{"x":-0.9,"y":0.7},"to":{"x":-0.4,"y":0.3}},{"kind":"vector","label":"Step 3","from":{"x":-0.4,"y":0.3},"to":{"x":0,"y":0}}]}}
```

To minimize this error, we compute the gradient, which is a vector of partial derivatives pointing toward the steepest ascent.

We then take a step in the exact opposite direction, scaled by a hyperparameter called the learning rate. This iterative updating continues until the parameters converge near the local minimum.

prompt: what is the difference between precision and recall?
title: Precision and Recall Matrix
body:
Precision is defined as $\frac{TP}{TP + FP}$ and measures the exactness of positive predictions made by a model. It asks how many of the selected items were actually relevant.

Look for the predicted positive row in the matrix to see how false positives penalize precision.

```rh-diagram
{"version":1,"diagram":{"title":"Confusion Matrix for Precision and Recall","caption":"Precision divides true positives by predicted positives, while recall divides true positives by actual positives.","kind":"matrix","columns":["Actual Positive","Actual Negative"],"rows":[{"heading":"Predicted Positive","cells":["True Positive (TP)","False Positive (FP)"]},{"heading":"Predicted Negative","cells":["False Negative (FN)","True Negative (TN)"]}]}}
```

Recall is defined as $\frac{TP}{TP + FN}$ and measures the completeness or sensitivity of a model. It asks how many of the actual positive items the model managed to capture.

Notice that recall uses the actual positive column, meaning false negatives are the primary penalty here.

prompt: How does successive halving decide which trials get more training?
title: Successive Halving Allocation
body:
Successive halving evaluates a pool of hyperparameter trials on a small initial budget, ranks them by a validation metric, and discards the bottom half.

The surviving trials receive a larger resource allocation for the next round, repeating this prune-and-promote cycle until one configuration remains.

Look at the evaluation matrix below to see how trials are ranked and filtered at each cumulative step.

This mechanism aggressively shifts computational budgets toward the most promising trials without wasting time on poorly performing runs.

body:
When processing the token sat, a transformer starts with its combined embedding and position vector. This vector holds the semantic meaning and location of the word in the sequence.

```rh-diagram

Input embedding transforms into query, key, and value vectors.","kind":"transformation","before":{"label":"Input for sat","items":[{"tensor":{"rows":1,"columns":4,"dimensions":"1 × 512","name":"Embedding plus position","values":[1.109,-0.516,0.72,1.4],"role":"input"}}]},"after":{"label":"Projected vectors","items":[{"tensor":{"rows":1,"columns":2,"dimensions":"1 × 256","name":"Query","values":[1.829,-0.516],"role":"output"}},{"tensor":{"rows":1,"columns":2,"dimensions":"1 × 256","name":"Key","values":[1.109,1.4],"role":"output"}},{"tensor":{"rows":1,"columns":2,"dimensions":"1 × 256","name":"Value","values":[0.72,1.4],"role":"output"}}]},"operation":"Multiply by the learned weight matrices","links":[{"from":0,"to":0},{"from":0,"to":1},{"from":0,"to":2}]}}

To drive attention, the model multiplies this input vector by three separate learned weight matrices. These linear projections produce the query, key, and value vectors for the attention head.

Each projected vector serves a distinct role in the upcoming dot-product calculations.

The query looks for relevant tokens, the key advertises what the token contains, and the value holds the actual information to be passed along.

prompt: Why does a transformer use more than one attention head?
title: Why Transformers Use Multi-Head Attention
body:
When translating the sentence The cat sat on the mat, a single set of attention weights struggles to track both syntactic grammar and local noun-verb links at the same time.

Multi-head attention solves this by splitting the hidden dimension into parallel projection subspaces called attention heads, allowing each head to focus on a different type of relationship.

Head A learns to connect the verb sat directly to its subject cat, capturing semantic action.

Head B instead attends to structural determiners like the first occurrence of the, preserving word order and syntax.

prompt: how are attention weights computed?
title: Computing Attention Weights
body:
Attention weights determine how much focus one token places on another during sequence processing. Consider a query vector $q$ comparing against key vectors $k_i$ across the input sequence.

We compute their raw compatibility using the dot product score $s_i = q \cdot k_i$.

Look for the normalized allocation of these scores in the diagram below.

```rh-diagram
{"version":1,"diagram":{"title":"Weights on words","caption":"The weights sum to one after softmax normalization.","kind":"token-links","source":["red","kite"],"target":["red","kite"],"queries":[{"index":1,"weights":[0.25,0.75]}],"normalized":true}}
```

These raw scores are then divided by the square root of the key dimension $\sqrt{d_k}$ to stabilize gradients. Passing these scaled scores through a softmax function produces the final attention weights that sum to one.

Multiplying these weights by the value vectors $v_i$ yields the final context output.

prompt: How does rescaling a personality score help explain embedding coordinates?
title: Rescaling personality scores for embedding coordinates
body:
When analyzing vector embeddings, raw features often have mismatched scales that distort distance metrics. By applying standardization, we shift each trait so its mean is zero and its variance is one.

This ensures that every coordinate contributes equally to cosine similarity calculations.

```rh-diagram

On the centered scale, the same result sits on the positive side.","kind":"number-line","min":-1,"max":1,"markers":[{"value":0,"label":"Middle of the original scale"},{"value":0.6,"label":"Jun’s centered sociability"}]}}
```

Consider a personality score like sociability measured from 0 to 100. Subtracting the population mean and dividing by the standard deviation transforms this raw mark into a standardized value.

Look at the marker for Jun's centered sociability in the diagram above to see how the score moves relative to the origin.

Embedding spaces rely on isotropic distributions to compute meaningful semantic neighborhoods.

prompt: what is batch normalization?
title: Batch Normalization
body:
Batch normalization stabilizes neural network training by recentering and rescaling layer activations.

Internal covariate shift occurs when intermediate layer distributions change during training, forcing later layers to constantly adapt.

Look at the formula in the diagram to see how each input feature is adjusted by its mini-batch statistics. The mini-batch mean $\mu_B$ and variance $\sigma_B^2$ are computed dynamically for every training batch.

```rh-diagram
{"version":1,"diagram":{"title":"Batch Normalization Transformation","kind":"transformation","before":{"label":"Input Activations","items":["Mean $\\mu_B$","Variance $\\sigma_B^2$"]},"after":{"label":"Normalized Outputs","items":["Mean 0","Variance 1"]},"operation":"$\\hat{x}_i = \\frac{x_i - \\mu_B}{\\sqrt{\\sigma_B^2 + \\epsilon}}$"}}
```

Subtracting the mean and dividing by the standard deviation produces normalized values with zero mean and unit variance. A small constant $\epsilon$ prevents division by zero during this standardization step.
